EWC helps retain the knowledge acquired from the original masked language modeling task by penalizing changes to weights deemed important for this task. We propose to further pre-train LMs on two novel tasks that involve negation. The first task is the Next Sentence Polarity Prediction (NSPP) task, where given a sentence, the model predicts whether the next sentence will contain negation. The main contributions of this paper are:

- Introducing two novel self-supervised tasks for pre-training LMs for negation.   
- Creating a large-scale dataset ( $\approx$ 6.4M samples) for these tasks.   
- Showing that further pre-training BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) independently on these tasks improves performance on CondaQA (Ravichander et al., 2022) and eight other negation-related benchmarks. CondaQA, to the best of our knowledge, is the largest corpus that requires reasoning over negation. It consists of 14,182 question-answer pairs and over 200 unique negation cues. # 2 Related Work

Negation understanding studies have focused on various aspects of negation, including negation detection (Khandelwal and Sawant, 2020; Truong et al., 2022; Morante and Daelemans, 2012), scope detection (Qian et al., 2016; Jumelet and Hupkes, 2018; Fancellu et al., 2017; Morante and Daelemans, 2009; Li and Lu, 2018; Zhao and Bethard, 2020), and focus detection (Rosenberg and Bergler, 2012; Shen et al., 2019; Zou et al., 2014, 2015).

Recent studies have also focused on improving the performance of LMs when negation is present. Sarabi et al. (2019) introduced affirmative inter

d Daelemans, 2009; Li and Lu, 2018; Zhao and Bethard, 2020), and focus detection (Rosenberg and Bergler, 2012; Shen et al., 2019; Zou et al., 2014, 2015).

Recent studies have also focused on improving the performance of LMs when negation is present. Sarabi et al. (2019) introduced affirmative interpretations, i.e., paraphrasing negated sentences without using negation cues. Hossain and Blanco (2022) and Rezaei and Blanco (2024) showed that incorporating affirmative interpretations improves the performance of LMs on negation-related benchmarks. In this paper, we show that our pre-training strategies outperform affirmative interpretations on CondaQA. Unlike theirs, our pre-training does not add any complexity at prediction time.

Hosseini et al. (2021) propose to augment negation understanding with BERT by unlikelihood training and synthetic data generation. Singh et al. (2023) repeats the pre-training procedure of BERT (i.e., MLM and NSP) modified to improve negation understanding. They add negation cues to the original next sentences rather than choosing a random sentence. Unlike them, we do not always add negation; instead, we reverse the polarity of the second sentence for the NSP task. That is, half the time we add negation to the next sentence and half the time we remove it. We also introduce a novel task, Next Sentence Polarity Prediction (NSPP), which is not explored by previous work. As we shall see, our pre-training outperforms previous work.

# 3 Empowering Language Models Against Negation

We propose a self-supervised method to make LMs more robust against negation. Our approach is to further pre-train LMs on two tasks that involve negation. These tasks are the Next Sentence Polarity Prediction (NSPP) task and a variation of the well-known Next Sentence Prediction (NSP) task. None of these tasks require labeled data; any text corpora are suitable. Also, they are not specific to any domain or downstream task.

# 3.1 Next Sentence Polarity Prediction (NSPP)

We introduce NSPP as the task of predicting the polarity of the next sentence given the current sentence. Given a pair of consecutive sentences, $(S_{1}, S_{2})$ , the input to the model is only $S_{1}$ , and the output is a binary label indicating whether $S_{2}$ includes any negation cues or not. For example, consider the following pair of sentences:

$S_{1}$ : The weather report showed sunny skies.   
$S_{2}$ :But it didn't stay that way.

Given only $S_{1}$ , the model should predict that the following sentence includes negation cues.

# 3.2 Next Sentence Prediction (NSP)

NSP is a well-known task in LM pre-training as first introduced by BERT (Devlin et al., 2019). The NSP task is to predict whether two sentences are consecutive. Devlin et al. (2019) (a) used consecutive sentences from Wikipedia as positive examples and (b) chose a random sentence from the same article to replace the second sentence and create a negative example.

We propose a variation of the NSP task to improv

We propose a variation of the NSP task to improve negation understanding. For a pair of con

secutive sentences, $(S_{1}, S_{2})$ , we create the negative pair $(S_{1}, S_{2}^{\prime})$ where $S_{2}^{\prime}$ is obtained by reversing the polarity of $S_{2}$ . That is, if $S_{2}$ includes negation cues, we remove them, and vice versa.

# 3.2.1 Reversing Polarity

We define rules to add and remove negation cues from sentences. These rules are used to create the negative pairs $(S_1, S_2')$ in the NSP task. To streamline the process, we only work with sentences that

- include not, $n't$ , or never as negation cues;   
- the negation cue modifies the main verb;   
are not questions; and   
- contain exactly one negation cue.

To develop the rules, we collected a large set of sentences from the English Wikipedia corpus (Wikipedia-Foundation, 2024) that met these criteria. We then generated the dependency tree for each sentence with spaCy (Honnibal and Montani, 2017; Honnibal and Johnson, 2015) and analyzed the frequency of outgoing edges from the main verb. Afterward, we manually inspected the most frequent tokens associated with each edge and leveraged these patterns to develop the rules below.

We evaluated these rules by manually inspecting 100 samples. In $96\%$ of them, the rules correctly reverse polarity. Note that the goal here is not $100\%$ correctness—it is to automatically generate data for pre-training with our tasks.

Adding negation. For sentences where the main verb has no auxiliary verb, we insert the negation cue directly and adjust the verb for tense and subject agreement. The cue never is always placed directly before the main verb. We append $n$ 't and not directly after the main verb if it is one of the following: were, was, is, are, do, will, would, may, might, shall, should, can, could, or must. For example, given the sentence "I was shopping," we add not to create the sentence "I was not shopping."

If the main verb is a gerund or present participle, we do not add $n$ 't directly to it; instead, we place not right before the verb. For present or past participles, we replace it with its lemma and insert the appropriate form of do before the lemma, ensuring it matches the tense of the verb and person of the subject. For present participles, we add do or does, and for past participles, we add did. We then insert not or $n$ 't after the auxiliary verb. For example, given the sentence "I went to the store," the main verb went is replaced with did not go, resulting in "I did not go to the store."

If the main verb has an outgoing edge labeled aux or auxpass in the dependency tree, we add the negation cue to the auxiliary verb. For example, given the sentence "The store is closed," we

ent to the store," the main verb went is replaced with did not go, resulting in "I did not go to the store."

If the main verb has an outgoing edge labeled aux or auxpass in the dependency tree, we add the negation cue to the auxiliary verb. For example, given the sentence "The store is closed," we add $n$ 't to the auxiliary verb is to create the sentence "The store isn't closed." However, for certain auxiliary verbs such as might and may, it is not possible to add $n$ 't directly to them. In such cases, we only add not or never to the sentences. Appendix A lists the auxiliary verbs we work with and the rules for adding each negation cue.

Additionally, to have more natural sentences with negation cues, we replace modifiers such as already and some with yet and any, respectively.

Removing negation. We begin by removing the negation cue from the sentence and adjusting the grammar accordingly. If the negation cue is $n$ 't (as in can't or won't), we remove $n$ 't and replace the auxiliary verb with its lemma (e.g., can and will).

Next, we remove any extra auxiliary verbs and adjust the main verb based on tense and subject agreement. If the auxiliary verb is did, we remove did and use the past tense form of the main verb. For example, given the sentence "I did not go to the store," we remove did and update go to went, resulting in "I went to the store". We apply the same process for do and does. That is, we replace the main verb with its base form or third-person singular form, respectively.

We also replace negative polarity items such as yet, at all, and any with their affirmative counterparts (already, somewhat, and some, respectively.) Lastly, if but functions as a conjunction and is a sibling of the main verb in the dependency tree, we replace it with and.

A note on using LLMs. Although using LLMs is expensive and time-consuming, we attempted to use state-of-the-art LLMs to reverse the polarity of sentences. We used the Llama-2 model (Touvron et al., 2023) and the GPT-4 model (OpenAI, 2023). We tried several prompting approaches to instruct the models to only add or remove negation cues without modifying other parts of the sentence. However, the models consistently made additional modifications to keep the meaning of the sentence intact. We hypothesize that this is because we work with Wikipedia sentences, which are typically about facts. Since these models are believed to be trained to be truthful, they often refuse to generate text that contradicts real-world facts. See examples of the prompts and outputs in Appendix B.

# 3.3 Dataset

We begin by extracting all sentences from Wikipedia containing negation that are not the first sentence of a section, ensuring that each has a preceding sentence $(S_{1})$ to provide context for the next sentence $(S_{2})$ . Next, we retain only the sentences where our rules for reversing polarity can be applied. We also extract affirmative sentences (i.e., without negation cues) along with their preceding

ection, ensuring that each has a preceding sentence $(S_{1})$ to provide context for the next sentence $(S_{2})$ . Next, we retain only the sentences where our rules for reversing polarity can be applied. We also extract affirmative sentences (i.e., without negation cues) along with their preceding sentences $(S_{1})$ . To ensure the sentences are truly affirmative, we verify that none of the negation cues from CondaQA are present. Additionally, we aim to select the same number of affirmative sentences from the same article as the negated sentences. If this is not possible, the remaining sentences are drawn from a different article. We obtain an equal number of negated and affirmative sentences, resulting in a total of $\approx 6.4\mathrm{M}$ $(S_{1}, S_{2})$ pairs. The negated and affirmative sentences are used as the positive and negative examples for the NSPP task, respectively. Next, we create $(S_{1}, S_{2}^{\prime})$ pairs by reversing the polarity of the $S_{2}$ sentences. We add only one negation cue to the affirmative sentences and ensure that we have the same distribution than in the negated sentences for each article.

We randomly choose 25,000 $(S_{1}, S_{2})$ pairs along with their corresponding $(S_{1}, S_{2}^{\prime})$ pairs to create the validation sets for pre-training. Half of the $S_{2}$ sentences are negated and the other half are affirmative. The NSPP task does not need the $(S_{1}, S_{2}^{\prime})$ pairs. Therefore, the validation sets consists of 25,000 and 50,000 pairs for the NSPP and NSP tasks, respectively.

# 4 Evaluation Benchmarks

We evaluate off-the-shelf LMs and versions further pre-trained with our strategies on benchmarks that require reasoning over negation. We primarily evaluate on CondaQA (Ravichander et al., 2022) and provide results on eight other relevant benchmarks. All the corpora that we work with are in English.

# 4.1 CondaQA

CondaQA (Ravichander et al., 2022) is a contrastive question-answering dataset. It is designed to evaluate the ability of models to reason over negation. The corpus consists of 14,182 question-answer pairs. Each question is paired with a passage that contains the answer to the question. Answers to questions are either Yes/No/Don't Know, a span in the question, or a span in the passage.

It was created by extracting 1,289 passages from the English Wikipedia which contained negation phrases. They started with a collection of negation cues (Morante et al., 2011; van Son et al., 2016) and expanded them. There are over 200 unique negation cues in CondaQA, including single-word (e.g., not, never), affixal (e.g., un-lucky, in-correct), and multi-word negation cues (e.g., a lack of, instead of). They also include several parts of speech tags such as verbs (e.g., refuse), nouns (e.g., absence), adjectives (e.g., uninterested), and adverbs (e.g., incorrectly).

Importantly, Ravichander et al. (2022) demonstrated that CondaQA cannot be solved by models relying solely on questions, edit types, or cues. This ensures that the dataset is free from artifacts that models could exploit to solve the task.

We evaluate our models on the CondaQA dataset using the accuracy and group consistency metrics. The term group refers to the original passage and either all three or one of the edited passages. Group consistency measures the percentage of questions answered correctly for all the passages in a group. Group consistency is arguably more important, as being robust against negation means being able to answer the question correctly with all original and edited passages.

Pre-training data for these tasks can be generated from any text corpus, and the tasks do not require any human annotations. Our experiments showed that further pre-training BERT and RoBERTa models on these tasks consistently improves their performance on a range of negation-related benchmarks, particularly on the challenging CondaQA corpus. Notably, while both NSPP and NSP tasks are beneficial, the NSP task yields consistently stronger improvements than the challenging NSPP task. Perhaps surprisingly, training on both tasks jointly does not provide further benefits. Future research could explore additional model architectures and pre-training corpora beyond Wikipedia or include more contextual information (more than two sentences) in the pre-training tasks. # Limitations We experiment with two models, RoBERTa and BERT, and a single pre-training dataset, Wikipedia. Future work may consider other models and pretraining datasets. Our rules for reversing polarity only cover "not", "n't", and "never". However, they are still effective in making models more robust against negation in general—recall that CondaQA has over 200 unique negation cues. Future work may consider working with more sophisticated rules to reverse the polarity of the sentences. We also only experiment with models pre-trained on 500K and 1M instances. Future work may consider training on the whole corpus and evaluate the performance on downstream tasks. Additionally, all the corpora we work with are in English. We acknowledge that negation may be expressed differently in other languages and this work may not generalize to other languages. We note, however, that the proposed tasks are language-agnostic and can be applied to other languages. # Ethics Statement The work in this paper does not involve human subjects. # D NLU and NLI Corpora

QNLI (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) is a natural language inference dataset created from the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) (Rajpurkar et al., 2016). It contains questions and sentences that are answers to other questions from SQuAD. The task is to determine whether the context sentence contains the answer to the question. WiC (Pilehvar and Camacho-Collados, 2019) is a word sense disambiguation dataset. It contains sentence pairs where a word can have the same or different meanings in the two sentences. The task is to determine whether the word has the same meaning in the two sentences. WSC (Levesque et al., 2012) is a coreference resolution dataset. It contains sentences where a pronoun can refer to different entities in the sentence. The task is to determine whether a pronoun and a noun phrase are co-referential.

# E LAMA and LAMA-Neg

The LAMA (Language Model Analysis) dataset, introduced by Petroni et al. (2019), serves as a probe for evaluating the factual and common

sense knowledge embedded within pre-trained language models. It consists of facts structured as subject-relation-object triples or question-answer pairs, which are transformed into cloze-style sentences to test whether language models can predict the correct masked token. LAMA encompasses various knowledge sources covering a range of factual and commonsense relations.

SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) the ability of models to answer natural language questions by transforming them into cloze-style sentences. Google-RE<sup>3</sup> assesses the ability to retrieve facts about dates, places of birth, and places of death. TReX (Elsahar et al., 2018), which contains a larger set of relations derived from Wikidata, challenges the models on their ability to generalize across a broader range of facts, although some noise exists due to the automatic alignment to Wikipedia. ConceptNet (Speer and Havasi, 2012), on the other hand, tests commonsense reasoning by providing facts about everyday concepts and relationships.

LAMA-Neg, introduced by Kassner and Schütze (2020), extends the LAMA dataset by incorporating negated instances to evaluate the ability of pretrained language models to handle negation. The dataset transforms positive cloze statements from LAMA int

For evaluation on LAMA and LAMA-Neg, we do not fine-tune the models, as these tasks lack dedicated training sets. Notably, since both LAMA and LAMA-Neg are masking tasks, it is crucial to prevent catastrophic forgetting during further pretraining. To address this, we apply Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) regularization (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) with a coefficient of $\lambda = 1e - 3$ . EWC helps retain the knowledge acquired from the original masked language modeling task by penalizing changes to weights deemed important for this task. This regularization ensures that while the model adapts to new tasks during pre-training, it preserves essential knowledge required for effective performance on the masking tasks. This strategy allows us to evaluate the models reliably on LAMA and LAMA-Neg without compromising their original capabilities. # G Ablation Study on Reversing the Polarity Recall that our pre-training data includes reversing the polarity of sentences, i.e., half the time we add negation to the original data and half the time we remove negation from the original data. In this section, we provide an ablation study to understand the effect of reversing the polarity of sentences on the performance of the models.
